Senses.PreferredTarget: open the way and let the encounter proceed
AlternateTargets: let pass rather than hold fast
give the other side room to move
Senses.Explanation: In a public encounter, to open the way and allow movement instead of blocking or holding fast. The recurrent contrast is with “hold fast” or “hold in place,” and the records make the difference visible through their own images. Tianzhang Yuanshan says that holding fast freezes dripping water and stops the rivers, while releasing brings warm sun, mild wind, and mountains and streams competing in beauty; he then asks which is good. Xuedou Chongxian says that under release rubble shines, while under restraint true gold loses color. Yinyuan Longqi opens a cloth bag, opens one road of release, and lets the assembly jump east and west before asking which is release and which is restraint. Tiantong Hongjue Min is asked for “a releasing saying” after the restraining side is set aside; he answers, “open in all directions.” Yuanwu Keqin asks whether releasing for people or holding them fast is good. Wumen Huikai says that holding fast and releasing each puts out one hand to raise the ancestral vehicle. Yongjue Yuanxian contrasts Boshan Wuyi, who only knew how to hold fast, with his own release on that day. The phrase has 1,034 occurrences in 224 allowlisted texts.
Senses.Note: Corpus counts: 1,034 hits in 224 texts. Attested formations include 'release, then...' (放行則), 151 hits in 80 texts; 'drawing in and releasing' (收放), 310 in 143; 'holding fast and releasing' (把定放行), 15 in 13; 'a road of release' (放行一路), 7 in 6; 'what is release...?' (如何是放行), 11 in 11; and 'not release' (不放行), 40 in 36. No exact definitional formula of the forms 'X means release' or 'is called release' was found. The two hits for 'one who releases' (放行者) are predicative uses, not definitions.
